title: Silverbolt
mood: A gray training frame, a year of salvage and one storm night: how Selena built the machine only she can ride.

hero.alt: The silver head of Selena's dragon-shaped machine Silverbolt, a tall crest above blue crystal eyes, blue light in its seams.

segs.t: Selena sat cross-legged on the tiles with a screwdriver in her hand and a lollipop in her cheek. Silverbolt lay beside her with its left hind leg across her knees, the knee plate open. The rain had not come yet.
She gave one screw a quarter turn. Blue light woke along the seams of its back. Deep in its chest the motor hummed like a purr.
“Better?”
The claws on that foot flexed once.
The pull lay toward the bay tonight, strong even under the thunder. She kept her back to it and closed the knee plate.
The first time Silverbolt ran on that leg, the leg came off.
The Science Division. Her first year.
The frame came to her bench in her first week.
It was an Academy training frame, compact and gray: a seat and a core on two squat legs. The tag on its side read FRAME NINE, and under that, SELENA.
“Registered to you,” said Chang’e. Standing, she was no taller than its seat. “Rule. No change to a registered mecha without a field-test report and my mark.”
“Any change?”
“Any.”
“Paint?”
“Especially paint.”
The first night the workshop emptied, Selena laid her palm on Frame Nine’s core.
Every suit at the Academy ran on belief. A pilot’s aspirant power lit the core, and the core moved the suit.
She held her hand there a long time. The core stayed dark.
Of course,
she thought.
There’s nothing in me it wants.
She took her hand away and pulled the crate of salvage out from under her bench.
That same week Selena crossed the courtyard and slowed down. A girl went past in cat ears. A boy on the steps wore a pair of curled horns.
On the way home she bought a dark headband shaped like a horned crest.

The next morning, in the alley behind the gate, she pinned it on. Then she let her own two horns grow up through her hair in front of it. She had kept them drawn in since she was small. The air was cold on them.
Finally.
At the gate only one boy looked twice. “Nice. Where’d you get those?”
“Grew them.”
He laughed and went on.
Before Karina’s stair she pulled them back in and put the headband in her bag.
Near the end of her first term she tried a stair nobody used. It climbed past the bell to a hatch. She shouldered the hatch up and climbed out onto the tiles.
The whole city lay under her, out to the dome’s edge. Beyond it the bay ran gray to the sky.
Mine,
she thought.
On the warm tiles she unwrapped a lollipop and let it melt down to the stick. Selena never bit one.

Over that year, late, after the lab had gone home, she rebuilt the frame. Every part came from her own salvage, out of dead Enders. Four legs and a long tail: the shape she had drawn on the back of her entrance paper. Big machines were slow, so she kept it small and low, a dragon’s shape just long enough to ride.
A report went in for every part she changed. In the box for material, each one read
salvage plating
, like every suit in the building. Chang’e marked them all.
The night she bolted on the last plate, she laid her palm on the core. Still dark.
So she opened her hand over it and let the purple out.
It ran off her fingertips into the metal. Blue light came up along every seam, plate by plate, out to the tip of the tail.
The frame lifted its head. It turned toward her hand and stopped a finger’s width from her palm.
Selena did not move.
So there is something in me it wants.
She laid her hand on its brow and kept it there until the purple sank back under her skin.
It had no mind and no voice. It moved when she meant it to, before her hands did.
The tests went badly. On the test floor, at a full run, the left hind leg sheared off and skidded under a bench.
Selena watched it stop spinning. “Huh? It broke already?”
Chang’e looked up from her clipboard. “That was a leg.”
“A prototype leg.”
That evening a report reached Chang’e’s desk.
Left hind leg. Came off. Replaced.
Chang’e made her mark.
Late in the year the frame walked into Chang’e’s lab on its own four feet. Selena strolled in behind it.
Chang’e dropped her spoon into her pudding. “I want new gadgets!”
She climbed onto its back and took hold of the seat rails. “Go.”
It did not move.
“Forward. Walk. Please?”
Not even its tail twitched.
“Is it broken?”
“It’s particular.”
The gray-haired professor who had once set a dead pump on Selena’s bench leaned in the doorway. “Fine tuning,” he said. “Tuned to one pilot. The director’s gear is the same.”
Chang’e slid down and glared at it.
The first big storm after that came in off the bay at dusk.

Selena rode the frame out past the last lit streets of the outskirts, into blocks the raids had left without roofs. Rain came in sideways. She pulled off her uniform jacket and pushed it into the hollow under the seat.
She let the purple go. It spread up her arms, over her collarbones and up her throat. In that rain every ward camera showed only white.
She laid both palms flat on the frame’s back. The plates warmed under them, and the motor rose from a hum to a roar.
Then they ran.
Broken walls went past in flashes. The frame cleared a gap between two roofs in one leap. The left hind leg took the far ledge and held, its claws throwing sparks.
She lay flat along its neck and grinned.
Prototype leg.
Water sheeted off its plates. The wind tore at her breath.
A laugh came out of her by itself. She had never had to copy that one.
“Nothing matters more to me than my freedom!” she shouted into the storm.
Nobody can call me back.
Lightning struck an old water tower across the block. In the flash the frame’s plates went silver from nose to tail.
Silverbolt,
she thought.

segs.t: They stopped on top of a broken wall. She sat with the rain running off her face. Under her the machine ticked as it cooled. The purple lay along her arms, and she did not call it back.
She stayed until the storm moved off over the bay.
In the morning she filed a report, because a name was a change.
Frame Nine. Name: Silverbolt.
Chang’e read it twice and made her mark.
To everyone else, it was the product of everything she had learned at the Academy, a powerful weapon built to defend the city. They were amazed that Selena alone could operate it so well.
At the year’s showing it stood on a plinth in the hall, behind a rope and a crowd. A boy from the Combat Division leaned over the rope. “You’ll be a hero with that thing. You know that?”
Selena turned her lollipop over. “Champion of justice? Sounds like a real pain in the shoulders. I think I’ll pass.”
He laughed. That week her file gained a line:
Outstanding Student.
But only Selena knew the truth: Silverbolt was, in every sense, a weapon of the Enders.
She clicked her tongue, and it followed her up the tower stair.
In class she drew.

Her pen had a small star on its end. Her desk had a clear screen set into it. Line by line, over months, a suit of armor grew there: a pale shell with a mane like a crest, four blades floating free of the arms, joints that bent the way an Ender’s did.

media.alt: A pen draws a blue line across a dark grid and a hand twirls a pen with a gold star on its end; then on graph paper a pale armored suit grows line by line, a crested helmet, a purple mane and four blades floating beside its arms.

segs.t: “Suit design?” asked the girl at the next desk.
“Something like that.”
Chang’e stopped behind her chair on the way past. “Excellent homework.”
Selena drew the shape she felt folded small under her skin when the purple came out on storm nights. She knew every plate of it from the inside.
She had never once let it all the way out.
She added a line to the left shoulder and kept drawing.
On the tower the first drops hit the tiles.
Selena pocketed the screwdriver and stood. Out over the bay, the pull leaned on her. She swung onto Silverbolt’s back and turned it away from the bay.

It dropped off the edge claws first, onto the roof of the hall below. The left hind knee took the landing without a sound. Then the next roof. The storm broke over them. Ahead, the whole city lay open in the rain, out to the dark of the outskirts.
